I. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy was thrown under the bus often enough to know how much
it hurts. Wiser after the experience of the US abandoning him in arms supply as well as
withdrawing intelligence support in war, Mr Zelenskyy played the supplicant to perfection,
even abiding by a sartorial ceasefire as he came to the White House. The marked contrast
between the upbeat mood of Monday in Washington when Mr Zelenskyy came with the
physical and moral support of virtually the whole of Europe, EU and NATO and the insipid
one-sided nature of the Alaskan Trump-Putin meeting of Friday can be interpreted to imagine
there is a birth of hope towards the Ukraine war ending. Of course, it is still in Russian President
Vladimir Putin’s hands as he is the one holding all the cards after he impassively withstood
Trump’s charm offensive at the military base in Anchorage.

A bright positive to emerge from the summit of leaders of the “coalition of the willing” and Mr
Trump and Mr Zelenskyy was that there will be security guarantees for Ukraine, possibly even
American boots on the ground to ensure that any peace agreement is adhered to after more of
the Donbas region, which is not quite in control of Russian troops yet, is given away in
exchange for peace everywhere, beginning with Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Mr Trump has
scuppered Ukrainian dreams of joining NATO, but American guarantees of security could
mean almost as much, as it could preclude Mr Putin from starting a war in the future, perhaps
at least so long as Mr Trump stays in the White House until January 2029. If a peace deal that
is elusive only due to Mr Putin’s intransigence is struck and Mr Zelenskyy delivers on his
promise of holding fresh elections, a rosy scenario can be envisaged.

All the theatre and the flattery appeared to pay off with the Europeans serving up a masterclass
in dealing with an egotistical Mr Trump. There may be something there for India as well since
it is left facing a huge Trump tariff trauma. But, if the war does stop, and Russia becomes an
acceptable entity for the Western world again, there may be relief for India that was not able to
find a way to tweak Mr Trump to its liking and advantage. Let the war end first.

questions.stimulus:
II. "Throughout the 1970s, Italy was convulsed by a series of bomb attacks, political
kidnappings and assassinations" carried out by left-wing terrorists, said Ian Thomson in the FT.
Of the groups that operated during the anni di piombi ("years of lead"), the "most feared" was
the Brigate Rosse (Red Brigades), which "combined a Marxist-Leninist utopianism with a


murderous disregard for human life". During its "18-year reign of terror", the group killed
around 75 people and maimed hundreds. Its highest-profile victim was former prime minister
Aldo Moro, who was kidnapped in March 1978 and whose bullet-riddled body was found 55
days later in the boot of a Renault 4.

Now John Foot, a professor of history at Bristol University, has written a "grimly absorbing"
history of the brigatisti and their attempts to overthrow the Italian state. As his "superbly
researched" book shows, the group subjected Italy to "some of the bloodiest acts of terrorism
yet seen in an industrialised society" – all for nothing, as they never came close to realising
their goals. Their story, Foot observes, amounted to a "national tragedy". The Red Brigades
was founded in 1970 by Renato Curcio, a student in Trento, his girlfriend (later wife)
Margherita Cagol, and Alberto Franceschini, a communist from Reggio Emilia. "Its roots,
however, lay much deeper," said Simon Gaul in Literary Review – in disquiet at America's
influence over Italy, growing industrial unrest in the country's northern heartlands, and a belief
that neo-fascists were plotting a military coup.

At first, the Red Brigades was backed financially by Giangiacomo Feltrinelli, the "increasingly
activist publisher of 'The Leopard' and 'Doctor Zhivago'", said James Owen in The Times. But
that source dried up in 1972, when Feltrinelli blew himself up while trying to detonate an
electricity pylon outside Milan. Italy in the early 1970s had an "epidemic of kidnaps by
organised crime groups", and the brigatisti jumped on this bandwagon, said Simon Heffer in
The Daily Telegraph. They first targeted industrialists or minor officials, but widened their net
to include prominent politicians. And they upped the violence, adding kneecappings and
executions to their repertoire ("Strike One to Educate 100" became their mantra). Eventually,
it became clear the group were "killing just because they could" – and as public support seeped
away, they turned on each other, and finally disbanded in 1988. Based on exemplary
scholarship, Foot's book provides a "fascinating insight" into these "moronic" fanatics.

IV. No more Mr Nice Guy. Five years after the Covid pandemic forced employers to embrace
empathy and flexibility, bosses are back to laying down the law. Tough talk is everywhere:
JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon blasted remote workers for being hard to reach on Fridays while
Google co-founder Sergey Brin insisted in a memo that “60 hours a week is the sweet spot of
productivity”.

The shift goes beyond talk. The shifting balance of power between companies and their
workers has multiple roots. The political context certainly favours bosses: US President Donald
Trump has publicly questioned the value of the federal work force, let go thousands of
government employees and ended collective bargaining for 1mn more. He is also reshaping the
National Labor Relations Board, which enforces worker-protection rules, by firing its chair and
adding two members that unions describe as “anti-worker”. The economic backdrop has also
strengthened management’s hand. While US unemployment remains relatively low, many
workers who do not like their jobs cannot readily find alternatives. US-based companies have
announced more than 800,000 job cuts so far this year, the most since the height of the
pandemic. Companies have been further empowered by the rapid rise of large language models
and other artificial intelligence. Many employers are holding off on hiring new workers while
they wait to see whether AI can make their existing workforce more productive — or replace
labour entirely.

Still there are limits to the amount of control that employers can exercise over their employees.
Employees have countered the demands for an always-on, ever-present workforce with a series
of subversive strategies. Social media is full of terms such as “coffee badging”, slang for
showing up to the office just long enough to swipe in and grab a cuppa, and “quiet vacationing”
— scheduling emails and setting up automatic responses to disguise time away. Strict rules,
demands for long hours and lay-off threats may boost corporate bottom lines initially, but there
are big risks to this strategy. AI is great for routine tasks, processing data and simple coding.
But more complex work will still require humans for the foreseeable future, and people with


top skills remain in high demand. On the flip side, bosses who bang on about how loyalty is
passé should not be surprised when their top people start to act like star athletes and offer
themselves to the highest bidder. If you are still counting on humans to handle your company’s
most complicated and high-stakes decisions, it seems like a poor strategy to alienate them
ahead of time.

not easy to find in ordinary light.” When his daughter Clara’s beloved black cat Bambino
disappeared while she was convalescing in a sanatorium, Mark Twain put out the ad in the
New York American and spent days receiving strangers with abandoned black cats in the hope
of finding Bambino among them. The cat returned on his own, but it was no secret in New York
that the American writer loved his daughter, and Bambino, with equal fervour.

That they occupy a special place in the lives of their humans is no secret. But separated by
centuries and continents, the spurt in litigation and mediations in India’s capital over pets and
strays only goes to show that the law is just beginning to catch up with what the heart has
always known: That animals matter — not as assets, but as companions. And, in some
circumstances, they are the bone of contention or caught between adversaries. Take, for
instance, a civil suit filed in 2023 by an advocate against his neighbours in south Delhi. The
reason: Their pet had chased him, leading him to fall and fracture his wrists. When TMC MP
Mahua Moitra broke up with lawyer Jai Anant Dehadrai, the bitterness spilled over into a
custody tussle over their beloved Rottweiler, Henry.

It may seem trivial to some, absurd even, but these disputes, at their core, are declarations of
how much trust is conveyed through a wag of a tail or the flick of a feline ear. In lonely, crowded
urban metropolises, pets provide the kind of unstinting comfort that few can. Neighbours fight,
lovers part, but what lingers is the bond with the creature left in between. Reforms to Australian
law last month recognised this: For the first time, in cases of separation, Australian courts will
factor in emotional attachment when determining pet ownership. As Delhi courts navigate this
tricky terrain, it is a reminder that love, no matter how small or furry, always leaves a trail.

X. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a bailment creates a relationship of trust and specific
reciprocal obligations. While the bailee’s duty of care is paramount, the law concomitantly
imposes several critical duties on the bailor to ensure fairness and facilitate the purpose of the
bailment. Primarily, the bailor has a duty to disclose faults in the goods bailed, a obligation
detailed in Section 150. This duty varies significantly based on the nature of the bailment. In
a gratuitous bailment (for the sole benefit of the bailee), the bailor is bound to disclose only
known faults that could expose the bailee to an “extraordinary risk.” Conversely, in a non-
gratuitous or reward-based bailment, the standard is stricter; the bailor is liable for any defect,
whether known or unknown, which materially interferes with the intended use of the goods,
effectively implying a warranty of fitness.

Furthermore, the bailor bears financial responsibilities. As per Section 158, in a gratuitous
bailment, the bailor must repay the bailee all necessary expenses incurred for preserving or
protecting the bailed goods. This ensures the bailee is not out of pocket for acting in the
bailor’s interest. A more profound duty arises from the bailor’s title to the goods. Section 164
stipulates that if the bailor has no valid title to the goods and the bailee consequently suffers a
loss—such as being compelled to deliver the goods to the true owner—the bailor is under a
duty to indemnify the bailee for such loss. This protects an innocent bailee from the
consequences of the bailor’s defective ownership.

Finally, the bailment relationship concludes with the duty to receive back the goods upon the
fulfilment of its purpose or the expiry of its term, as implied under Section 164. A refusal to
accept the returned goods would unjustly extend the bailee’s liability and possession. Thus,


the bailor’s duties—ranging from disclosure and indemnity to acceptance—form an essential
framework that supports the bailee’s performance and upholds the equitable foundations of
the contract of bailment.

XI. In a significant jurisprudential shift, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court has recalled
its own 2025 Vanashakti judgment, which had imposed an absolute prohibition on ex post facto
or retrospective Environmental Clearances (ECs). This ruling acknowledges the complex
tension between uncompromising environmental protection and pragmatic developmental
imperatives.

Ex post facto ECs refer to approvals granted after a project has commenced operations or
construction without the mandated prior clearance, effectively regularizing a violation. The
Vanashakti judgment had correctly identified these as an "anathema" to core environmental
principles, notably the precautionary principle enshrined in the Environment (Protection) Act,
1986, and EIA Notifications, which mandate prior assessment to prevent harm. It struck down
government instruments permitting such regularisation as a "gross illegality."

However, the recalling bench, in a 2:1 decision, held that the absolute ban was per incuriam—
rendered without due care for binding precedents. It highlighted that coordinate benches in


Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) and D. Swamy (2021) had, while discouraging the practice,
allowed regularization in exceptional circumstances with stringent penalties. The Court
invoked the principle of proportionality, reasoning that the remedy of demolition for procedural
lapses—where projects, often involving substantial public investment, began without EC due
to administrative delays rather than malafide intent—could cause disproportionate public harm.
It emphasized that the objective of environmental compliance could be achieved through heavy
monetary penalties and compulsory restoration measures, thereby bringing errant projects
under a regulatory umbrella without necessitating their wasteful destruction.

Consequently, the Court has referred the issue to a larger bench for authoritative reconciliation.
This move underscores a judicial attempt to balance ecological integrity with developmental
reality. It implicitly mandates that any future framework for exceptional ex post facto
regularisation must be coupled with robust deterrent penalties, rigorous monitoring via tools
like PARIVESH, and enforceable restoration obligations under the Polluter Pays Principle,
ensuring that expediency does not eclipse accountability.

XI. In a significant jurisprudential shift, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court has recalled
its own 2025 Vanashakti judgment, which had imposed an absolute prohibition on ex post facto
or retrospective Environmental Clearances (ECs). This ruling acknowledges the complex
tension between uncompromising environmental protection and pragmatic developmental
imperatives.

Ex post facto ECs refer to approvals granted after a project has commenced operations or
construction without the mandated prior clearance, effectively regularizing a violation. The
Vanashakti judgment had correctly identified these as an "anathema" to core environmental
principles, notably the precautionary principle enshrined in the Environment (Protection) Act,
1986, and EIA Notifications, which mandate prior assessment to prevent harm. It struck down
government instruments permitting such regularisation as a "gross illegality."

However, the recalling bench, in a 2:1 decision, held that the absolute ban was per incuriam—
rendered without due care for binding precedents. It highlighted that coordinate benches in


Alembic Pharmaceuticals (2020) and D. Swamy (2021) had, while discouraging the practice,
allowed regularization in exceptional circumstances with stringent penalties. The Court
invoked the principle of proportionality, reasoning that the remedy of demolition for procedural
lapses—where projects, often involving substantial public investment, began without EC due
to administrative delays rather than malafide intent—could cause disproportionate public harm.
It emphasized that the objective of environmental compliance could be achieved through heavy
monetary penalties and compulsory restoration measures, thereby bringing errant projects
under a regulatory umbrella without necessitating their wasteful destruction.

Consequently, the Court has referred the issue to a larger bench for authoritative reconciliation.
This move underscores a judicial attempt to balance ecological integrity with developmental
reality. It implicitly mandates that any future framework for exceptional ex post facto
regularisation must be coupled with robust deterrent penalties, rigorous monitoring via tools
like PARIVESH, and enforceable restoration obligations under the Polluter Pays Principle,
ensuring that expediency does not eclipse accountability.

XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, meticulously defines offences but also incorporates
essential General Defences (Sections 76-106) that absolve or mitigate liability by negating the
requisite mens rea or justifying the act. These defences are fundamental to a just criminal
jurisprudence, recognizing that not every harmful act constitutes a crime. A key defence is
Mistake of Fact, where a person acting under a genuine and reasonable mistaken belief of fact
is excused, as it negatives criminal intention. Similarly, acts performed by judges or officers
pursuant to Judicial and Executive Acts are protected when done in good faith under court
orders or legal authority.

The IPC excuses harm caused by an Accident (Sec. 80)—a purely unfortunate event occurring
despite ordinary care and without criminal intent. Conversely, the defence of Necessity (Sec.
81) justifies an act done to prevent greater harm, provided the act was necessary and the harm
caused was proportionate. The law also prescribes exemptions based on capacity. Infancy
completely exempts a child below seven and conditionally those between seven and twelve, if
lacking maturity of understanding. Insanity (Sec. 84) is a complete defence, adhering to the
M’Naghten Rules, requiring proof that the accused, due to unsoundness of mind, was incapable
of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

Intoxication (Sec. 85-86) provides a nuanced defence. Involuntary intoxication can excuse if it
renders the person incapable of forming intent. However, voluntary intoxication is generally
no defence, except potentially for proving the absence of a specific intent in certain crimes. A
vital justificatory defence is the Right of Private Defence (Sec. 96-106), which empowers
individuals to protect their own or another’s body and property against imminent unlawful
aggression, subject to the cardinal principle of proportionality. Furthermore, Consent can be a
defence, but only if it is free, informed, and given by a competent person, and never for acts
intended or known to cause grievous hurt or death. Finally, the law disregards Trivial Acts (Sec.
95) causing harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain.


Collectively, these defences ensure the penal code punishes only blameworthy conduct,
balancing societal protection with individual justice.

XIII. The law of torts provides justifications or defences which, when successfully pleaded,
can absolve or mitigate a defendant’s liability, balancing the plaintiff’s right to compensation
against equitable exceptions. A foundational defence is Volenti Non Fit Injuria, which asserts
that one who voluntarily and knowingly assumes a risk cannot subsequently complain of the
harm. This applies to clear scenarios like participating in a contact sport, but courts scrutinise
the voluntariness and adequacy of consent, especially in employer-employee relationships.

Closely related is Contributory Negligence, where the plaintiff’s own failure to take reasonable
care for their safety contributes to the damage. Historically, this was a complete bar to recovery.
However, in India, through judicial evolution and statutory amendments like the Motor
Vehicles Act, courts now apportion liability using the principle of comparative negligence,
awarding damages reduced by the plaintiff’s share of fault.

Certain events negate human agency altogether. An Act of God (vis major) refers to an
overwhelming natural cause without human intervention, like an unprecedented flood, while
Inevitable Accident denotes an unexpected event despite all reasonable precautions. Both
defences succeed by proving the harm was unforeseeable and unavoidable. Justificatory
defences include the Right of Private Defence, permitting reasonable force to protect one’s


person or property from imminent threat, and Necessity, which excuses an act causing lesser
harm to prevent a greater, imminent danger—key distinctions being the source of the threat
and the absence of fault in necessity.

A complete defence is Statutory Authority, where the act complained of is expressly permitted
by law. Conversely, Mistake, whether of fact or law, is generally not a defence in tort, as
liability often hinges on the act itself, not the defendant’s subjective intent. Finally, the
procedural defence of Limitation is critical; a suit must be filed within the prescribed period
(typically one to three years from the date the wrong is discovered). Failure to do so
extinguishes the remedy, regardless of the merit of the claim, underscoring the law’s interest in
finality and diligence.

can absolve or mitigate a defendant’s liability, balancing the plaintiff’s right to compensation
against equitable exceptions. A foundational defence is Volenti Non Fit Injuria, which asserts
that one who voluntarily and knowingly assumes a risk cannot subsequently complain of the
harm. This applies to clear scenarios like participating in a contact sport, but courts scrutinise
the voluntariness and adequacy of consent, especially in employer-employee relationships.

Closely related is Contributory Negligence, where the plaintiff’s own failure to take reasonable
care for their safety contributes to the damage. Historically, this was a complete bar to recovery.
However, in India, through judicial evolution and statutory amendments like the Motor
Vehicles Act, courts now apportion liability using the principle of comparative negligence,
awarding damages reduced by the plaintiff’s share of fault.

Certain events negate human agency altogether. An Act of God (vis major) refers to an
overwhelming natural cause without human intervention, like an unprecedented flood, while
Inevitable Accident denotes an unexpected event despite all reasonable precautions. Both
defences succeed by proving the harm was unforeseeable and unavoidable. Justificatory
defences include the Right of Private Defence, permitting reasonable force to protect one’s


person or property from imminent threat, and Necessity, which excuses an act causing lesser
harm to prevent a greater, imminent danger—key distinctions being the source of the threat
and the absence of fault in necessity.

A complete defence is Statutory Authority, where the act complained of is expressly permitted
by law. Conversely, Mistake, whether of fact or law, is generally not a defence in tort, as
liability often hinges on the act itself, not the defendant’s subjective intent. Finally, the
procedural defence of Limitation is critical; a suit must be filed within the prescribed period
(typically one to three years from the date the wrong is discovered). Failure to do so
extinguishes the remedy, regardless of the merit of the claim, underscoring the law’s interest in
finality and diligence.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. The recent India Justice Report starkly exposes the systemic failures impeding India’s
juvenile justice framework, revealing a profound gap between the rehabilitative ideals of the
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and its implementation. The most
critical failure is the high pendency of cases, with over 55% of matters before Juvenile Justice
Boards (JJBs) pending, directly contradicting the Act’s mandate for speedy, child-centric
inquiry. This delay is exacerbated by structural gaps in JJB constitution, where 24% of boards
lack full membership, undermining quorum and informed decision-making. Compounding this
is the absence of legal services clinics in 30% of JJBs, violating children's right to timely legal
aid and fair procedure.

These operational deficiencies are rooted in deeper systemic administrative weaknesses,
including poor inter-agency coordination and a stark lack of transparency, evidenced by weak
RTI compliance. The absence of a unified National Data Grid fragments oversight, preventing
effective monitoring across police, child protection services, and legal authorities. While the
2015 Act marked a progressive shift by establishing JJBs for rehabilitation and empowering
CARA for adoption, its potential is neutralized by these bottlenecks. The 2021 Amendment,
which made certain offences non-cognisable and empowered District Magistrates in adoption,
addresses symptoms but not the core infrastructural crisis.

Consequently, urgent reform measures are imperative. Strengthening institutional
infrastructure by ensuring fully staffed JJBs with attached legal clinics is foundational. The
focus must pivot decisively from custodial approaches to robust rehabilitation and reintegration


within Child Care Institutions (CCIs), supported by vocational and psychological services.
Ultimately, creating a centralized public data portal is essential for tracking pendency,
monitoring child welfare, and enforcing accountability. Without these interventions, the
legislative promise of a justice system that prioritizes the child’s best interest and dignity
remains unfulfilled, perpetuating procedural injustice over protection.

questions.stimulus:
XV. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is the definitive statute governing intestate succession
for Hindus, including Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs. It establishes a uniform and secular code,
replacing the traditional textual law of the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga schools. Its primary
objective is to systematize the rules of inheritance, bringing clarity and gender justice to the
devolution of property.

The Act's applicability extends to any person who is a Hindu by religion, in any form, including
Virashaivas and Lingayats, and to those belonging to the religions mentioned. A core feature
of the Act is the creation of a statutory hierarchy of heirs, supplanting the traditional sapinda
and gotraja systems. This hierarchy is structured into four tiers: Class I heirs, Class II heirs
(listed in an order of precedence), Agnates, and Cognates. Class I heirs, such as the widow,
mother, son, daughter, and descendants of pre-deceased children, take precedence
simultaneously, excluding all others. Only in their absence do subsequent categories inherit.

Central to the Act's operation is the concept of the coparcenary, a distinct entity within a Joint
Hindu Family comprising a common ancestor and his lineal male descendants within three
generations. The revolutionary 2005 Amendment accorded the daughter the status of a
coparcener by birth, granting her rights and liabilities equal to a son. Coparcenary property
refers to ancestral property in which each coparcener holds an undivided, birthright interest.
This contrasts with separate or self-acquired property, which an individual procures through
personal effort, free from ancestral lineage.

Upon the death of a coparcener, the mechanism of notional partition is invoked. This legal
fiction deems a partition of the coparcenary to have occurred immediately before the member's
death, crystallizing his share. This ascertained share then devolves not by survivorship to the
remaining coparceners, but by testamentary disposition or, in its absence, via intestate
succession under the Act to his own legal heirs. This intricate interplay between the law of
coparcenary and the statutory scheme of heirs ensures a structured and equitable distribution
of a Hindu's estate.

questions.stimulus:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.

In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.

In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,


hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Computers can’t surprise”, aeon.]

questions.stimulus:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.

In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.

In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,


hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.

[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Computers can’t surprise”, aeon.]
